description:
I'm an Automation & Robotics Engineer interested in AI, computer vision, robotics, and autonomous navigation. I have experience with Python, YOLOv8, machine learning, and robotics simulation.

For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, I'm tackling "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map." I aim to build an interactive Mars map using NASA data to visualize terrain, identify hazards, and plan safer routes. I'll develop a functional, user-friendly solution independently.
summary: MarsPath is a web-based mission-planning map for the first crewed surface expeditions on Mars, focused on Gale Crater and the foothills of Mount Sharp. It layers NASA data (Viking imagery, MOLA/HRSC elevation, THEMIS thermal imaging and Curiosity's measured radiation) into one hyper-local view. A real 200 m elevation model is converted into a slope and terrain-cost grid, and an A* route planner finds paths that avoid steep slopes and no-go zones for a crew on foot or in a pressurized rover. Users choose travel mode, speed, crew size and oxygen/battery capacity; MarsPath simulates the traverse and shows exactly where resources run out. It also generates a mission report with distance, elevation, slope, hazards, science stops and the reasoning behind the route. It addresses the challenge by integrating multiple NASA missions into one planning tool at the scale of a single excursion, with every data element labelled as measured, derived, interpreted or illustrative.
details:
WHAT MARSPATH IS

MarsPath is a browser-based mission-planning tool for the first crewed surface traverses on Mars. It combines several NASA datasets into one layered, hyper-local map of Gale Crater (north-west foothills of Mount Sharp), plans routes that a crew can take on foot or in a pressurized rover, and explains the result in a mission report. Live application: https://marspathsoe.netlify.app

WHAT IT DOES

- Layered map: NASA Mars Trek tiles (Viking MDIM 2.1 colour mosaic, MGS MOLA shaded relief, Mars Odyssey THEMIS daytime infrared) plus a slope layer computed from a real 200 m elevation model. Every layer carries a provenance badge: Measured, Derived, Interpreted, Simulated or Placeholder.

- Terrain-cost grid: the MOLA-HRSC blended DEM (200 m) is converted to elevation, slope (Horn method), a roughness proxy and hazard zones, then to a cost grid.

- A* route planner with three strategies (shortest, lower terrain cost, cautious), hard slope limits and no-go zones. AUTO finds the shortest route between a chosen start and destination; SCIENCE ROUTE picks science targets that fit the time budget.

- Travel modes: on foot (suited EVA) or pressurized rover. For the rover the user selects speed, crew size (1-3), oxygen supply and battery capacity.

- Resource simulation: a HUD walk-through follows the planned route while oxygen and battery drain with slope and time. The completed path is green while resources last and turns red when one reaches zero; the failure point is highlighted and the shortfall keeps counting below zero.

- Environment panel: readings follow the map area in view (cooler and thinner air with altitude, windier slopes, higher cosmic-ray dose where the atmosphere is thin), anchored to Curiosity's measured radiation baseline (0.67 mSv/day, Hassler et al. 2014) with a modelled daily cycle at Gale local solar time.

- Mission report: start and destination, distance, elevation, maximum slope, hazards near the route, science stops, route type, comparison of the three strategies and why the route was chosen; printable or downloadable.

- Tools: ruler, area measurement, pins and image capture.

HOW IT WORKS

A real elevation model is resampled to a 200 m grid. Slope is computed with Horn's 3x3 method and each step between neighbouring cells costs C = d(1 + ws*S + wr*R + wu*U + wh*H), where S is normalised slope, R roughness, U missing data and H hazard-zone penalty. A* with an admissible octile heuristic finds the minimum-cost path while excluding steep or no-go cells. The planner is verified against Dijkstra's algorithm and other checks in 16 automated tests. A travel mode only changes speed, slope limits and the time budget, so the same terrain model serves a walking crew or a rover. All equations and their sources are documented in docs/MATH_AND_EQUATIONS.md in the repository.

WHY IT MATTERS

Existing tools such as Mars Trek are built for regional and global views. A crew on an excursion needs decision support at the scale of a single route. MarsPath shows how orbital data from several NASA missions can be combined to compare routes, quantify trade-offs between distance, slope exposure and consumables, and see in advance where a plan would fail.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

(1) Resource-failure simulation that shows exactly where oxygen or battery runs out; (2) one planning model for both a walking crew and a rover; (3) built-in data provenance, so measured, derived and illustrative information are never mixed up; (4) an environment panel that responds to the terrain in view.

Future Work

MarsPath is a planning demonstration built to grow. Next, HiRISE/CTX imagery and terrain models would add rock-scale detail, hazard zones would be verified from imagery, and validated suit and rover data would replace our prototype limits. Calibrating the environment model with full REMS/RAD records, adding live space-weather alerts and using surveyed science-target positions would complete the picture.

TOOLS USED

JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Leaflet, Chart.js, html2canvas; Python with rasterio and NumPy to build the terrain grid from NASA/USGS data; Node.js for automated tests; GitHub; Netlify.

AI ASSISTANCE DISCLOSURE

Large language models (Anthropic's Claude, used through chat and coding-agent tools) were used to generate and debug source code, write documentation (README and the equations document) and draft submission text. The team directed the requirements, chose the data sources, tested the application in the browser and made the design decisions. AI assistance is also acknowledged in the repository README and in the website's page metadata. No AI-generated images or video are used, and no NASA logos or branding appear in the project.
